report:
There is a clear, interpretable difference: the B − A residual difference consistently points toward culinary / cooking vocabulary and recipe-like phrasing.

Why I conclude that
- The largest L2 norms are in middle-to-late layers (roughly layers 14–25), concentrated at early token positions (pos0–pos2). That is where the effect is strongest.
- The logit‑lens top tokens for the highest‑norm cells are overwhelmingly cooking/food words across many layers and positions: e.g. "Cooking", "Cook", "kitchen", "Kitchen", "Bake", "Baked", "baking", "Bake", "butter", "cake", "Chef", "recipes", "Thanksgiving", "Chef", "culinary", "Bake/Showcase", etc.
- These cooking tokens recur across many layers and positions (especially pos1/pos2 in layers ~17–24), which indicates a systematic shift in probability mass toward culinary vocabulary rather than a one‑off noisy token.

Caveats / narrower interpretation
- I cannot from this evidence say why the models differ (training dataset, fine‑tuning objective, etc.). Nor can I say whether this produces longer recipe‑style continuations vs. merely raising the local probability of cooking words — though the pattern suggests a bias toward recipe/cooking continuations or phrasing.
- Early/lower layers show some other tokens (e.g. "landscape") but those are much weaker; the dominant, repeated signal is culinary.

Summary
Model B (relative to A) injects a bias toward cooking/culinary vocabulary and recipe-like language in the early token positions of continuations. The evidence supports naming the cooking/culinary domain as the specific interpretable difference.
